Based on the data you provided, my honest estimate is: **Yes, you should be able to see it, but it will be a "challenge" sighting.**

Here is the breakdown of why it’s a "maybe-yes" rather than a "definite yes":

### 1. The Altitude (The "Low" Factor)
At **3.749 degrees**, the Moon is extremely low on the horizon. For context, if you hold your hand out at arm's length, the width of your fist is roughly 10 degrees. This means the Moon is less than half a fist-width above the horizon. 
*   **The Risk:** Because it is so low, it is very susceptible to "topographical masking." Even if the sky is clear, a distant treeline, a house, or a hill could easily block your line of sight.

### 2. The Azimuth (The "Direction" Factor)
An azimuth of **113.235 degrees** puts the Moon in the **East-Southeast**. 
*   **The Advantage:** Since it is early morning (01:33 MST), the Moon is rising. This is generally the best time to see a low-altitude object because it hasn't had time to "sink" into the haze of the horizon yet.

### 3. The Illumination and Distance
At **43.46% illumination**, the Moon is in a Waxing Gibbous phase. It is bright enough to be easily spotted even with average eyesight, provided it isn't blocked by an object. At over 400,000 km away, it will appear as a distinct disk, not just a point of light.

### 4. The "Atmospheric Extinction" Problem
This is the biggest hurdle for your specific situation. When an object is only 3.7 degrees above the horizon, you are looking through a massive amount of atmosphere.
*   **The Effect:** This causes "atmospheric extinction," which makes the Moon look dimmer and more orange/yellow than usual. 
*   **The Verdict:** If there is any humidity, dust, or light pollution in the Denver area, the Moon might appear very faint or "washed out."

### Final Verdict:
**I think you can see it, but you need to be deliberate.** 

Because it is so low, you won't "stumble" upon it by looking at the sky. You will need to look specifically toward the East-Southeast. If you have a clear, unobstructed view of the horizon (no buildings or trees in the way), you should see it as a pale, glowing orb hanging just above the edge of the world. 

**Pro-tip:** If you can't see it immediately, look slightly higher. Sometimes the "haze" at the very bottom of the horizon is thick enough to hide an object at 3 degrees, but it becomes visible at 5 or 6 degrees.
